GameStop Tumbles 8% Despite Ryan Cohen’s $26M Insider Buy; eBay Ticks Up
Ryan Cohen just put $26 million of his own money into GameStop shares, yet the stock is sliding hard anyway. The question now is whether that insider conviction holds the monthly rally together or profit takers win the argument.
Published September 25, 2026, 10:56am ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The exterior of a GameStop store, symbolizing the company's unexpected financial strength and potential for strategic acquisitions. © GameStop Logo Sign - Vallejo - California (CC BY 2.0) by Will Buckner
Chief executive Ryan Cohen disclosed a $26 million purchase of GameStop (NYSE:GME | GME Price Prediction) shares in a regulatory filing earlier this week, putting his own money behind the retailer at recent levels. GameStop stock is down 8% to $23.11 in morning trading, a drop that still leaves the shares up 29% over the past month.
The VanEck Video Gaming and eSports ETF (NASDAQ:ESPO) is down 0.8%, a much softer dip for a fund that holds GameStop among its gaming names. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.11% to $768, leaving the broad market essentially steady. GameStop stock is falling far harder than both funds, which keeps the pressure centered on its own crowded positioning.
Ryan Cohen’s filing showed he bought roughly 1.1 million GameStop shares, and the stock rose once the disclosure became public. That purchase is several sessions old, which means GameStop shares are trading on how holders handle the gain it produced.
The drop in GameStop stock reflects profit taking after that sustained run. Holders who followed Cohen into the shares are booking part of their gains, and the modest declines in the gaming fund and the S&P 500 fund show that selling hasn’t spread beyond this one name.
Within the VanEck fund, GameStop shares made up 4.3% of net assets as of June 30, a mid-sized weighting in a portfolio led by larger game publishers. The rest of the portfolio leans on names such as Capcom, Konami and Bandai Namco, and that mix is posting only a softer decline. That gap shows the selling in GameStop stock is specific to the retailer.
The SPDR fund’s slip is far too small to explain a move of this scale in GameStop shares. Crowded positioning in GameStop stock, built during the monthly run, can amplify an unwind once holders start taking profits, and the stock’s own behavior is carrying the loss.
GameStop’s most recent quarterly profit got a lift from its stake in eBay (NASDAQ:EBAY), a holding of roughly 43.4 million shares valued at $4.9 billion. Earlier this year, GameStop made an unsolicited bid for eBay, which eBay rejected. The retailer has also reduced debt by swapping bonds for company stock, a path that avoided paying out cash. eBay stock is up 0.47% to $108.34.
Weighing Cohen’s Signal Against the Pullback
The optimistic argument for GameStop begins with who bought the shares. A chief executive putting personal money into the shares at recent levels is the least ambiguous signal an insider can send, and the purchase ties Cohen’s fortunes more closely to those of other holders. GameStop also lists its dependence on Ryan Cohen among its risk factors, emphasizing how central he is to the story.
Timing is the problem for GameStop. The stock has given back part of what it gained on the news, so the signal has been priced and then partly reversed. GameStop’s latest quarterly report also flags the concentration of its investment portfolio in eBay common stock as a risk, tying part of the company’s value to a single outside holding.
Whether the monthly gain in GameStop stock holds without a fresh reason to own the shares is what these figures don’t settle. Cohen’s buy, the eBay position and the debt swaps are all known quantities, and none of them is new information. That leaves GameStop shares leaning on sentiment until the company offers its next update.
It is worth watching for any new disclosure from GameStop on its eBay stake or on insider buying, since either could give the shares another reason to move. A second purchase from Cohen would reinforce the original signal, while a quiet stretch could let profit taking run further.
Swings of this magnitude in GameStop stock reward discipline. Anyone adding GameStop shares on the drop ought to stay small, and holders already sitting on gains should size their exposure with that volatility in mind. Setting an exit level in advance can keep a sharp reversal from turning into an oversized hit to their portfolio.
Stocks that fall this hard against a steady market can reverse quickly in either direction. For GameStop, the insider purchase confirms conviction at the top of the company, and the next test for the stock is whether its monthly advance lasts without a new catalyst.

eBay started as a one-person experiment, too. What to value when starting small
Nemoto here!
When we hear stories about large companies, it can feel like they were people from a different world from the very beginning. They had amazing technology, massive amounts of capital, and a clear path to success. We assume that's why they were able to do it.
However, I feel that by looking only at the finished product, we distance ourselves from the actions we can take today. This time, I would like to think about what we should verify in a small business, starting from the origins of eBay.
The entrance to a large market was an individual's trading experiment
The founder of eBay is Pierre Omidyar. In his biography submitted to the SEC, it is explained that he started it as a sole proprietorship in September 1995 and incorporated it in May 1996. You cannot equate the current size of the company with its form at the time of founding.Founder and Management Biography from eBay's 2006 SEC Filing
The initial site was named AuctionWeb. In a letter from the founder in February 1996, he noted that since launching on Labor Day of the previous year, usage had spread beyond his imagination, and he had come to feel that it was a major experiment in testing commercial transactions on the Internet.Pierre Omidyar's Founder Letter dated February 26, 1996
What attracts me to this is the fact that a grand success story wasn't already complete at the start. First, you create a place for transactions. People come there. Interactions occur. By watching those reactions, you gradually see what is needed next.
Of course, just because you know how eBay started doesn't mean that doing the same thing will lead to the same result. The times and the competition are different. However, we can also re-question whether we need to keep increasing our preparations before verifying someone's reaction.
Starting small is different from starting sloppily. Even if you are handling just one product, you still need to confirm its condition, provide a description, determine how to deliver it, and commit to communication. Scaling down is not about letting go of that responsibility, but about creating a scope that you can verify yourself until the end.
Before asking "Did it sell?", what do you want to verify?
For example, suppose someone starting an overseas sales business first researches a single product. If they decide at this point that "if it doesn't sell in a week, I'm not cut out for this," they will overlook what they could have learned. Are they failing to use the words buyers are searching for? Is the condition not being conveyed? Do the price and shipping terms not match? You cannot understand the cause from the result alone.
If it were me, I would first write down just one thing I want to verify with this action. For example, "Can the scratches on this product be conveyed to the other party through photos and descriptions alone?" For that purpose, you can not only increase the number of photos but also have a third party look at them and ask where it is difficult to make a judgment.
The action of generating sales and the action of understanding the state in which you can generate sales are not always the same. If you think about this separately, I think the pain of feeling like your entire self is being evaluated by a single reaction will decrease a little.
I also want to decide the scope of the trial in advance. The time I can use, the amount of money I can put into inventory, the place where I can store items, and the time I can spend answering inquiries. If you expand your experiment to the point of breaking your daily life or commitments, you may find yourself unable to continue before you get any results.
This is not a story about making your dreams small. It is a story about choosing a step that the current you can take responsibility for, in order to continue while protecting the things you love. Precisely because you have resolve, you want to think about a form that allows you to continue.
Turn today's step into a record that allows for the next judgment
What you can do today is make a single memo about the product or service you want to test. "Who do I want to help and with what?" "How is that person doing now?" "Where am I verifying this time?" If you can write these three things in your own words, it becomes easier to determine the priority of your preparations.
After executing, separate what you did from the other party's reaction and keep a record. I changed the description. I retook the photos. There was an inquiry. How many hours did it take to respond? If you keep a record of what actually happened, not just your own impressions, you can choose where to change next.
The less reaction you get, the more you might want to change everything at once. But if you change the product, the price, and the description, you won't know which change was relevant. If it were me, I would fix things one by one, starting from the parts where the reason for review is clear. Of course, problems related to safety or misdescription are handled first.
Before you start, I think it's good to decide when you will look back. The purpose of setting a period is not to decide quickly whether it is a success or a failure. It is to verify what you have learned and what you still do not know using the time you have decided upon. Even if there is no reaction, you can specifically leave behind where to look and the order in which to try things.
Before deciding to "increase products because they aren't selling," you can return to those notes. If you can't keep up with managing the current number, increasing them isn't necessarily the answer. I want to be able to choose the next step based on what I've learned, rather than on a whim.
Another thing I want you to keep track of is what was inconvenient for the customer. Even if you think you've explained it well enough, it might be too long for the other person, or the necessary information might be buried at the end. When you're at a small stage, it should be easier to fix those inconveniences with your own hands.
What I want to cultivate in my business is not just the single event of a sale. It's about the people involved being able to make their own decisions next time, and being able to move forward with more peace of mind than before. I believe that this accumulation is what gives meaning to running a business.
It would be a waste to use the history of eBay only to look at an amazing company. Even for those of us who aren't big yet, we can take action today to reduce one inconvenience. Let's leave that step behind in a way that leads to tomorrow's decisions.

Boston, MASSACHUSETTS, Sept. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Blancco Technology Group, the industry standard in data erasure and mobile lifecycle solutions, today announced its participation in an eBay Live charity auction initiative led by its customer Quick Ship Brands, a certified reverse logistics, refurbishment, and IT asset disposition company. Blancco donated the diagnostics and certified data erasure software licenses to ensure every donated smartphone, laptop, and desktop could be safely repurposed for the auction.
In an unprecedented effort for the company, Quick Ship donated 100% of the hammer proceeds from electronics they auctioned through eBay Live – a real-time, interactive livestream shopping experience where buyers can bid on and purchase items as they are showcased.
Quick Ship's inaugural charity auction, held on September 16, benefitted Jonathan's Landing Foundation, a 501c3 nonprofit that builds neuroinclusive housing and workforce pathways for adults with autism, intellectual and development disabilities, and other neurodiversities. To date, the charity has raised $150,000 from the auction, including corporate donations and commitments landed after the show.
"We want to thank Blancco for donating the device diagnostic and data erasure software so that each item crossing the screen is verified, sanitized and buyer-ready," said Jordan Insley, founder and CEO of Quick Ship Brands. "We are also thankful for the credentialing organizations CTIA and WISE; they are a key reason a refurbished device carries real trust behind it. And of course, we couldn't serve worthwhile organizations like Jonathan's Landing at this scale without our industry partners. Ryan Cohen wrote a personal check for a million shares of his own company. The filing dated September 10, 2026 shows the purchase at $20.3759 per share, and a director bought the same day. The stock settled the most recent session at $24.04, up 5.62%.
GameStop (NYSE:GME | GME Price Prediction) sales keep sliding while a proposed takeover of eBay (NASDAQ:EBAY), a business several times its size, sits on the risk-factor page of the last 8-K. Open-market purchases with personal money are the most informative signal any insider can send. A chief executive writing a check for tens of millions while quarterly revenue falls almost 19% is likely seeing something the market hasn’t priced in yet.
Three directors bought in the same window: Lawrence Cheng, 55,000 shares at $18.7992 on September 8, James Grube, 10,255 at $19.12 on September 9, and Alain Attal, 5,000 at $20.00 on September 10.
Insider sells have a dozen reasons. Insider buys have one. A purchase at a higher price than the last one carries even more information.
The Q2 FY2027 8-K, filed September 8, 2026, discloses approximately 43.4 million shares of eBay common stock valued at approximately $4.9 billion and continues to reference the proposed acquisition of eBay in forward-looking risk factors.
The word that matters is proposed. The bid has never been formally withdrawn, and the company still flags that it may not be completed.
Revenue in the most recent quarter came in at $790.2 million, down 18.7% year over year, yet operating income jumped to $160.2 million, up 141.27%. Gross margin expanded to 43.7% from 29.1%.
Collectibles hit $356.3 million, up 57%, and now make up 45.1% of net sales. Video games fell to $263.2 million from $494.6 million.
However, I’d ignore the headline net income. It was flattered by a $166.3 million derivative gain tied to eBay and dinged by a $75 million loss on digital assets.
Balance Sheet, Guidance, and the Trigger
Against a market cap of $12.13 billion, GameStop carries $4.85 billion in cash and a $4.9 billion eBay position. A meaningful share of the equity value sits in marketable securities rather than in store operations.
Management raised the fiscal 2026 Adjusted EBITDA outlook to in excess of $650 million from in excess of $600 million. The trigger is a formal withdrawal of the eBay bid, a definitive agreement, or another Cohen buy at a price above $20.3759.
Bull: a chief executive spending real money on his own stock in a coordinated cluster with directors, a collectibles category growing fast enough to reshape the mix, record operating income for the period, and an investment portfolio no other specialty retailer can match.
Bear: total sales are still falling, the crypto position introduces volatility unrelated to the business, and the eBay bid may quietly evaporate into a passive stake that never becomes a deal.
The deciding variable is whether collectibles growth can outrun the legacy business’s decline before the market decides the eBay stake is just an expensive hedge fund position wrapped in a retailer.

What is the difference between eBay and Sekaimon? What you need to know to avoid losses on your first overseas purchase
As I continue to list items on eBay, I sometimes hear from Japanese buyers who say they use Sekaimon even though they suspect it might actually be cheaper to buy directly on eBay.
As someone who has been on the selling side of eBay for a long time, I have realized through my transactions that the experience of receiving an item can change significantly depending on how you buy it, even for the same product.
In this article, I will organize how eBay and Sekaimon work and what the differences are.
By the time you finish reading, you should have the information you need to decide which one you should choose.
What is the fundamental difference between eBay and Sekaimon?
eBay is an auction and flea market platform where sellers from all over the world list items directly and buyers purchase them directly.
On the other hand, Sekaimon is a service that allows you to view and purchase eBay listings in Japanese, and handles everything from the purchase to international shipping and customs clearance to Japan. service.
In other words, Sekaimon is not eBay itself, but is positioned as an intermediary service that makes eBay products easier to use from Japan.
One reason this difference is hard to understand is that the products displayed on the Sekaimon purchase screen are actually items listed by eBay sellers.
There are many cases where the entry point for buying is different, but the source of the product itself is the same.
Even from my perspective as a seller listing items on eBay, there are actually not many situations where I am conscious of whether a buyer is using Sekaimon or buying directly through eBay.
However, because fees, supported languages, and shipping mechanisms differ significantly, the experience will change depending on which one the buyer chooses.
A typical case is assuming that Sekaimon is an official eBay service.
In reality, it is an independent intermediary service operated by a separate company, and its fee structure and support are also different.
Another is simply comparing the displayed price on Sekaimon to see if it is higher or lower than buying directly on eBay.
Since Sekaimon's fees include international shipping and customs procedures, it is easy to misjudge the actual profit or loss if you compare them without understanding the breakdown of the displayed amount.
I have also had several opportunities to explain this difference in mechanism when buyers asked me about pricing.
In the end, which one is right for you?
Based on what we have covered so far, the answer to the question of whether you should use eBay or Sekaimon comes down to the difference in priority between choosing based solely on low cost versus choosing based on peace of mind and convenience.
Using eBay directly is suitable for those who are comfortable with English correspondence and want to handle everything themselves, including direct communication with sellers and price negotiations.
On the other hand, intermediary services like Sekaimon are suitable for those who are uneasy about communicating in English and would rather prioritize the peace of mind provided by Japanese support and proxy services, even if it means paying some fees.
The key criteria for your decision are how much you can handle in terms of English correspondence, how you compare the total costs including fees, and which support you can rely on in the event of a problem—these three points.

Should You Buy eBay Stock For Its Cash?
eBay's (EBAY) free cash flow is 5.2% of its market value, against 4.6% for the median S&P 500 company. A stock usually offers more cash for its price than most for one of two reasons. Investors either underrate the business or expect its cash to shrink. A buyer needs to know whether eBay's cash is underrated or about to shrink.
eBay's free cash flow was $2.4 billion over the last twelve months, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier. Free cash flow is the cash left after a company pays its costs and funds its investment.
As a shareholder, you own a share of that cash whether or not eBay pays it out. Every $10,000 of eBay stock comes with about $520 of free cash flow a year. When investors value that cash more highly, the share price tends to follow. The effect is stronger when the cash is growing.
eBay earns revenue on the sales that pass through its marketplace. The revenue comes from fees, advertising and shipping services. In the second quarter of 2026, eBay kept 14% of the value of goods sold as revenue. The marketplace needs little investment. eBay spent $0.6 billion on capital investment out of the $3.0 billion its operations brought in over the last twelve months.
eBay's free cash flow was positive throughout the last three years, but it did not hold steady. Three years ago it was $2.4 billion, the same as today. It fell to $1.5 billion the following year before recovering.
eBay owes little against that cash. Net debt, which is debt minus cash, was $3.8 billion on its latest reported balance sheet. That debt is 8.1% of eBay's market value. eBay's operating profit is 9.9 times its interest bill.
Why Does eBay Stock Yield More Than Most?
eBay stock yields more partly because the price appears to assume its growth is slowing. The stock lost 7.5% over the past three months, while the S&P 500 returned 2.7%.
Management's own forecast shows a slowdown. Adjusted earnings per share grew 17% in the second quarter of 2026. For the third quarter, management guided growth of 1% to 5%.
On its August 5, 2026 call, management explained the slowdown from the second quarter to the third. Most of it comes from harder comparisons with last year, management said. A year ago, eBay had the benefit of the launch of its U.S. Klarna partnership and of triple-digit growth in Pokémon. Both make comparisons in 2026 tougher.
eBay also bought Depop, a resale business, for $1.4 billion in cash on July 30, 2026. Management expected two effects from Depop in the third quarter. Depop would add about 2.5 points to currency-neutral growth in the value of goods sold. The purchase would also take 3 to 4 points off adjusted operating income growth.
eBay's operating margin, its operating profit per dollar of revenue, has already slipped. The margin was 20.5% over the last twelve months, down from 21.3% a year earlier. Even so, management raised its full-year outlook on the August 5 call. Management also expects Depop to add to adjusted operating income in 2028.
Watch eBay's Earnings Growth Against Its Guide
Adjusted earnings growth above the 1% to 5% that management guided would be a sign that eBay's cash is still rising. Growth at the low end, with a lower operating margin, would be a sign of cash levelling off.
eBay's free cash flow is back at its level of three years ago. The risk is that eBay's cash stops rising as its earnings growth slows.
eBay can carry its debt: its operating profit is 9.9 times its interest bill. The open question is growth. The third-quarter 2026 results will show whether eBay keeps growing through harder comparisons and the cost of Depop.

pages.title: Buying And Selling Airbags On eBay Is Now A Thing Of The Past... And It's Probably For The Best
pages.text:
Image Credit: Rahul Pugazhendi / Unsplash.
Buying a replacement airbag from a stranger on the internet always required a certain amount of trust. Considering what happens when one of these safety devices fails, eBay has decided that trust isn't enough anymore.
As of September 24, 2026, eBay no longer permits sellers to list standalone airbags or airbag inflators. Steering wheel airbag covers are included in the prohibition as well.
The marketplace says the decision followed a comprehensive review of the risks these products can pose to users. The change arrives amid heightened scrutiny of dangerous replacement airbag components that have made their way into vehicles in the United States.
Recent findings from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration illustrate just how serious the consequences can be. The agency says one particular type of defective replacement inflator has now been connected to 11 deaths and three severe injuries.
Image Credit: Nebular / Unsplash.
eBay's new policy applies across its airbag category and prohibits any seller from offering airbags or inflators. Sellers were instructed to remove affected active, scheduled, and draft listings by September 24, with eBay saying it would remove remaining listings itself.
There are some exceptions for related components that don't actually contain an airbag or inflator. Outside the United States, items such as airbag control units, crash sensors, diagnostic modules, and passenger sensors can continue to be listed, while U.S. sales of those parts are restricted to currently pre-approved sellers.
Trying to relist prohibited equipment could result in selling restrictions. eBay says listings removed as part of the policy change won't negatively affect a seller's compliance history.
Defective Replacement Inflators Have Killed 11 People
The timing is notable given NHTSA's ongoing warnings about dangerous replacement airbags. In April, the agency took the unusual step of banning the sale and importation of certain frontal driver airbag inflators marked DTN60DB after determining that they contained a safety-related defect.
Instead of operating normally during a collision, the defective inflators can rupture and propel metal fragments into the passenger compartment. NHTSA's latest figures link them to 11 deaths and three severe injuries across 14 crashes in the United States.
The agency says the affected vehicles had previously received replacement driver-side frontal airbag inflators. Known incidents have involved Chevrolet Malibu, Hyundai Sonata, and Chevrolet Equinox models, although NHTSA says it has no information indicating the problem is limited to those vehicles.
This Is One Car Part You Don't Want To Get Wrong
Image Credit: Shutterstock.
Airbags rely on an extremely rapid deployment process to protect occupants during a collision. NHTSA estimates frontal airbags saved more than 50,000 lives over a 30-year period, illustrating just how valuable the technology can be when everything works properly.
The problem is that determining the history and authenticity of a replacement component purchased online isn't always straightforward. NHTSA recommends that owners whose vehicles previously experienced an airbag deployment have replacement equipment inspected by a reputable mechanic, particularly if the repair wasn't performed by the manufacturer's dealership.
Losing easy access to used airbags on eBay might be inconvenient for some repairers and enthusiasts. Still, when the part sitting inches from your face is designed to explosively deploy during a crash, this is one online bargain that's probably better left alone.

Chief executive Ryan Cohen disclosed a $26 million purchase of GameStop (NYSE:GME | GME Price Prediction) shares in a regulatory filing earlier this week, putting his own money behind the retailer at recent levels. GameStop stock is down 8% to $23.11 in morning trading, a drop that still leaves the shares up 29% over the past month.
The VanEck Video Gaming and eSports ETF (NASDAQ:ESPO) is down 0.8%, a much softer dip for a fund that holds GameStop among its gaming names. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.11% to $768, leaving the broad market essentially steady. GameStop stock is falling far harder than both funds, which keeps the pressure centered on its own crowded positioning.
Ryan Cohen’s filing showed he bought roughly 1.1 million GameStop shares, and the stock rose once the disclosure became public. That purchase is several sessions old, which means GameStop shares are trading on how holders handle the gain it produced.
The drop in GameStop stock reflects profit taking after that sustained run. Holders who followed Cohen into the shares are booking part of their gains, and the modest declines in the gaming fund and the S&P 500 fund show that selling hasn’t spread beyond this one name.
Within the VanEck fund, GameStop shares made up 4.3% of net assets as of June 30, a mid-sized weighting in a portfolio led by larger game publishers. The rest of the portfolio leans on names such as Capcom, Konami and Bandai Namco, and that mix is posting only a softer decline. That gap shows the selling in GameStop stock is specific to the retailer.
The SPDR fund’s slip is far too small to explain a move of this scale in GameStop shares. Crowded positioning in GameStop stock, built during the monthly run, can amplify an unwind once holders start taking profits, and the stock’s own behavior is carrying the loss.
GameStop’s most recent quarterly profit got a lift from its stake in eBay (NASDAQ:EBAY), a holding of roughly 43.4 million shares valued at $4.9 billion. Earlier this year, GameStop made an unsolicited bid for eBay, which eBay rejected. The retailer has also reduced debt by swapping bonds for company stock, a path that avoided paying out cash. eBay stock is up 0.47% to $108.34.
Weighing Cohen’s Signal Against the Pullback
The optimistic argument for GameStop begins with who bought the shares. A chief executive putting personal money into the shares at recent levels is the least ambiguous signal an insider can send, and the purchase ties Cohen’s fortunes more closely to those of other holders. GameStop also lists its dependence on Ryan Cohen among its risk factors, emphasizing how central he is to the story.
Timing is the problem for GameStop. The stock has given back part of what it gained on the news, so the signal has been priced and then partly reversed. GameStop’s latest quarterly report also flags the concentration of its investment portfolio in eBay common stock as a risk, tying part of the company’s value to a single outside holding.
Whether the monthly gain in GameStop stock holds without a fresh reason to own the shares is what these figures don’t settle. Cohen’s buy, the eBay position and the debt swaps are all known quantities, and none of them is new information. That leaves GameStop shares leaning on sentiment until the company offers its next update.
It is worth watching for any new disclosure from GameStop on its eBay stake or on insider buying, since either could give the shares another reason to move. A second purchase from Cohen would reinforce the original signal, while a quiet stretch could let profit taking run further.
Swings of this magnitude in GameStop stock reward discipline. Anyone adding GameStop shares on the drop ought to stay small, and holders already sitting on gains should size their exposure with that volatility in mind. Setting an exit level in advance can keep a sharp reversal from turning into an oversized hit to their portfolio.
Stocks that fall this hard against a steady market can reverse quickly in either direction. For GameStop, the insider purchase confirms conviction at the top of the company, and the next test for the stock is whether its monthly advance lasts without a new catalyst.

When we hear stories about large companies, it can feel like they were people from a different world from the very beginning. They had amazing technology, massive amounts of capital, and a clear path to success. We assume that's why they were able to do it.
However, I feel that by looking only at the finished product, we distance ourselves from the actions we can take today. This time, I would like to think about what we should verify in a small business, starting from the origins of eBay.
The entrance to a large market was an individual's trading experiment
The founder of eBay is Pierre Omidyar. In his biography submitted to the SEC, it is explained that he started it as a sole proprietorship in September 1995 and incorporated it in May 1996. You cannot equate the current size of the company with its form at the time of founding.Founder and Management Biography from eBay's 2006 SEC Filing
The initial site was named AuctionWeb. In a letter from the founder in February 1996, he noted that since launching on Labor Day of the previous year, usage had spread beyond his imagination, and he had come to feel that it was a major experiment in testing commercial transactions on the Internet.Pierre Omidyar's Founder Letter dated February 26, 1996
What attracts me to this is the fact that a grand success story wasn't already complete at the start. First, you create a place for transactions. People come there. Interactions occur. By watching those reactions, you gradually see what is needed next.
Of course, just because you know how eBay started doesn't mean that doing the same thing will lead to the same result. The times and the competition are different. However, we can also re-question whether we need to keep increasing our preparations before verifying someone's reaction.
Starting small is different from starting sloppily. Even if you are handling just one product, you still need to confirm its condition, provide a description, determine how to deliver it, and commit to communication. Scaling down is not about letting go of that responsibility, but about creating a scope that you can verify yourself until the end.
Before asking "Did it sell?", what do you want to verify?
For example, suppose someone starting an overseas sales business first researches a single product. If they decide at this point that "if it doesn't sell in a week, I'm not cut out for this," they will overlook what they could have learned. Are they failing to use the words buyers are searching for? Is the condition not being conveyed? Do the price and shipping terms not match? You cannot understand the cause from the result alone.
If it were me, I would first write down just one thing I want to verify with this action. For example, "Can the scratches on this product be conveyed to the other party through photos and descriptions alone?" For that purpose, you can not only increase the number of photos but also have a third party look at them and ask where it is difficult to make a judgment.
The action of generating sales and the action of understanding the state in which you can generate sales are not always the same. If you think about this separately, I think the pain of feeling like your entire self is being evaluated by a single reaction will decrease a little.
I also want to decide the scope of the trial in advance. The time I can use, the amount of money I can put into inventory, the place where I can store items, and the time I can spend answering inquiries. If you expand your experiment to the point of breaking your daily life or commitments, you may find yourself unable to continue before you get any results.
This is not a story about making your dreams small. It is a story about choosing a step that the current you can take responsibility for, in order to continue while protecting the things you love. Precisely because you have resolve, you want to think about a form that allows you to continue.
Turn today's step into a record that allows for the next judgment
What you can do today is make a single memo about the product or service you want to test. "Who do I want to help and with what?" "How is that person doing now?" "Where am I verifying this time?" If you can write these three things in your own words, it becomes easier to determine the priority of your preparations.
After executing, separate what you did from the other party's reaction and keep a record. I changed the description. I retook the photos. There was an inquiry. How many hours did it take to respond? If you keep a record of what actually happened, not just your own impressions, you can choose where to change next.
The less reaction you get, the more you might want to change everything at once. But if you change the product, the price, and the description, you won't know which change was relevant. If it were me, I would fix things one by one, starting from the parts where the reason for review is clear. Of course, problems related to safety or misdescription are handled first.
Before you start, I think it's good to decide when you will look back. The purpose of setting a period is not to decide quickly whether it is a success or a failure. It is to verify what you have learned and what you still do not know using the time you have decided upon. Even if there is no reaction, you can specifically leave behind where to look and the order in which to try things.
Before deciding to "increase products because they aren't selling," you can return to those notes. If you can't keep up with managing the current number, increasing them isn't necessarily the answer. I want to be able to choose the next step based on what I've learned, rather than on a whim.
Another thing I want you to keep track of is what was inconvenient for the customer. Even if you think you've explained it well enough, it might be too long for the other person, or the necessary information might be buried at the end. When you're at a small stage, it should be easier to fix those inconveniences with your own hands.
What I want to cultivate in my business is not just the single event of a sale. It's about the people involved being able to make their own decisions next time, and being able to move forward with more peace of mind than before. I believe that this accumulation is what gives meaning to running a business.
It would be a waste to use the history of eBay only to look at an amazing company. Even for those of us who aren't big yet, we can take action today to reduce one inconvenience. Let's leave that step behind in a way that leads to tomorrow's decisions.
